description: Real-world benchmark RWB-07 (entrypoint-unreached): ini.parse() is genuinely called in this source, but only from a function never reached by the configured {file, symbol} entrypoint.
reason: loadLegacyIniConfig() has a real, live, unconditional call to ini.parse() -- a naive grep for 'calls the vulnerable function' would wrongly flag it. But the configured entrypoint is {file: src/config.js, symbol: loadModernConfig}; loadLegacyIniConfig is not itself an entrypoint source, is never called by loadModernConfig, and is never called by anything else in this file. A human analyst reading this file, informed of the actual entrypoint, concludes with confidence this code path is not reachable from the application's real usage. Currently returns UNKNOWN instead -- a known, tracked gap, not a fabricated oracle. Real ini@1.3.5 exports 'parse' via a chained CommonJS alias (exports.parse = exports.decode = decode); the implementing function is named 'decode', not 'parse', so export-symbol attribution cannot resolve the rule's ini#parse target to any real function at all -- target attribution is correctly reported unresolved (UNKNOWN) rather than risking a coincidental match. Before VT-301B this same unresolved target fell through to a phantom node, which happened to read as NOT_AFFECTED only because loadModernConfig's own reachable subgraph is trivially edge-less -- not because the target was ever actually identified. See FINDINGS.md RWF-012.

description: Real-world benchmark RWB-09a (MULTI_INSTANCE, vulnerable instance): the vulnerable semver@7.5.1 instance, installed under the npm-aliased dependency name semver-vulnerable, reached via isLegacyCompatible().
reason: isLegacyCompatible() calls `new legacySemver.Range(userRange)` directly, where legacySemver is `require('semver-vulnerable')` -- a real npm-aliased install of the real semver@7.5.1 (confirmed: node_modules/semver-vulnerable/package.json declares "name": "semver", "version": "7.5.1", within GHSA-c2qf-rxjj-qqgw/CVE-2022-25883's vulnerable range 7.0.0-<7.5.2). A human analyst reading this file and the real package-lock.json has no ambiguity: this specific installed instance is reached. Currently returns NOT_AFFECTED instead of AFFECTED -- a known, tracked gap, not a fabricated oracle. Root cause (VT-302 investigation, once RWF-010's benchmark-hermeticity contamination was removed and this case could be diagnosed cleanly): identifyModule() derives a package instance's identity from its own installed directory name ("semver-vulnerable", the npm alias), not from the name its own package.json declares ("semver") -- so graphPackageInstances(graph, "semver") never associates this instance with the rule's "semver" target at all, and resolveTargetNodes treats it as confirmedAbsentInstance (VT-212's guard, meant for a genuinely-never-touched instance) even though it is genuinely reached. See docs/REAL-WORLD-BENCHMARK-AUDIT-V0.1.md RWF-009 (package-alias identity mismatch, not yet formally tracked as a numbered FINDINGS.md entry). RWF-004 (Range's cross-file re-export via require('./classes/range')) is a second, independent gap that would also block this case even if RWF-009 were fixed.

IMPORTANT -- this is a BENCHMARK DESIGN ISSUE, not a VulnTrace defect: the actual scan result is NO_FINDING (no findings entry at all for this instance), not an explicit NOT_AFFECTED verdict, because VulnTrace's buildFinding() correctly omits any finding when matchResult is confidently "not_affected" by version alone (verdict.ts's documented behavior). This case's expected value should arguably represent "no finding" rather than a verdict string; left unchanged here per instructions not to silently alter the oracle -- see FINDINGS.md's note on RWB-09b.

description: Real-world benchmark RWB-11a (VT-303: genuine nested multi-instance, reached instance): two distinct, real, unaliased url-parse installs exist (nested 1.4.7 under a fixture-authored wrapper package, reached via consumer.parseNested(); top-level 1.4.4, never imported). Only the nested instance is reached.
reason: checkNestedUrl() calls consumer.parseNested(rawUrl), which requires("url-parse") from inside node_modules/consumer -- Node's own nearest-node_modules resolution finds the NESTED node_modules/consumer/node_modules/url-parse@1.4.7 instance, never the fixture's own top-level url-parse@1.4.4. Unlike RWB-09 (which tests npm-ALIASED identity via a differently-NAMED install directory, semver-vulnerable), no aliasing is involved anywhere here: both instances are plain, differently-versioned, real published url-parse installs at different real paths, the exact shape npm itself produces for a transitive dependency needing a version its consumers don't share. Verified directly (hermetic execution): resolves to node_modules/consumer/node_modules/url-parse/index.js, packageId.name="url-parse" correctly (no identity mismatch), evidence path src/index.js -> consumer/index.js -> url-parse/index.js:177 (the Url constructor) -- the same target shape RWB-04 already proves resolves cleanly, chosen deliberately so the only mechanism under test is package-instance discrimination, not export attribution.

description: Real-world benchmark RWB-11b (VT-303: genuine nested multi-instance, unreached instance): same fixture as RWB-11a. The top-level url-parse@1.4.4 instance is a real, genuinely installed direct dependency, never imported by anything reachable from the entrypoint at all -- only the nested 1.4.7 instance (RWB-11a) is ever called.

Deliberately BOTH instances are vulnerable versions (1.4.4 and 1.4.7, both within GHSA-8v38-pw62-9cw2's real >=1.0.0 <1.5.7 range) rather than one vulnerable and one patched -- this keeps the test isolated to instance discrimination alone (VT-212/VT-300's confirmedAbsentInstance mechanism) rather than also depending on version-range matching, and avoids RWB-09b's own known NO_FINDING oracle-design limitation entirely (see FINDINGS.md). Verified directly (hermetic execution): the top-level instance is never discovered by the call graph, and the analyzer correctly reports NOT_AFFECTED for it even though 44 unrelated unsupported_construct edges exist elsewhere in url-parse's own internal implementation (none of them closure-widening, so VT-300's guard correctly does not intervene).
